RAILAY ACT, 1903.
House went Into committee to consider the following proposed resolutions:

That it is expedient to provide as follows with respect to the salaries of the board, and other expenses incidental to the carrying out of the provisions of the Bill, now before the House, to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways :-

column2: The chief commisisoner to be paid a salary, of $10,000 per annum.

The secretary to he paid a salary to be fixed by the Governor in Council, not more than $4,000.

Such salaries and remunerations to be paid to the other officers, staff and appointees of the board, and such other expenses to be paid incidental to the carrying out of the provisions of the Bill as are approved by the Governor in Council.

column1: 88117,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.2,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,"QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"I am sorry that the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is not in his seat at the momeut. He will be here soon. In the meantime, I may expose to the House the reasons' which have induced the government to suggest the salaries mentioned in these resolutions. These salaries are the highest that will be paid by the government for any officers that we have at the present time ; they are even higher than the salaries of the justices of the Supreme Court and superior courts of the land, higher also than the salaries of the ministers. It has been observed, and, I think, with a great deal of truth, that the salaries that are now paid to the highest judicial officers are becoming-indeed, have actually become-insufficient. No revision of such salaries has taken place for thirty-five years, since the opening of confederation ; and the opinion has been expressed more than once on the floor of this House

,,,The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).,
88118,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.3,1903-08-06,89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982,ca.m.3867,Hon. Mr. FIELDING.,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"in past sessions, and during the present session also, that the time has practically arrived when it would be advisable to have a revision of salaries paid to the judges. The commission which we are organizing will have to discharge duties of no less importance than the duties now discharged by the judges. Some of the officers, especially the chief commissioner will have to be versed in the law generallly and in the law of railways, and versed also in all matters which appertain the practical working of railways. That being so, it seems to us that the salaries proposed are not at all too high. In comparison with the salaries to be paid other officers, it may perhaps sound high, but, looking at it from the point of view of the importance of the duties which are to be discharged by these officers, and judging it also by what is done for the judges and other officers of the government, I think the House will be disposed to agree with us that what we ask them to vote is not at all unreasonable. If we compare the salaries we propose for these commissioners with the salaries that are paid to railway managers, for instance, whose duties are no higher or no more important than those assigned to the chairman of the Railway Commission, it will perhaps be agreed, that these salaries are reasonable. It must be borne in mind also that the gentlemen who serve on this commission will be denied many of the advantages which to-day appertain to the judicial office. For instance, the judges of the land are not removable, holding office during good behaviour. The members of the commission are appointed for ten years, and even during those ten years they are removable.

,Liberal,,William Stevens Fielding,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Graham Haggart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0161da2d-c63a-468c-a51e-070c1f9ee40f&Language=E&Section=ALL
88120,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.5,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"I feel assured that I am right in saying the term is ten years. But during those ten years the tenure of the office is not so secure as the tenure of the office of judges, becaitse they may be removed in the same manner as lieutenant-governors are removed. The judges are not removable except after very exhaustive proceedings, they can only be removed upon an address voted by both Houses of parliament. From this consideration it seems to us that the sum of $10,000 which we propose to be paid to the chairman of the commission, is an adequate salary. If this sum is agreed upon as a reasonable compensation to the person who is to act as chairman of the commission, then we submit also that the sum of $8,000 pari passu ought to be the salary to be paid to the other two commissioners.

,,,The PRIME MINISTER.,

88129,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.14,1903-08-06,a1231855-4bec-419e-9184-2deabd03d8a5,ca.m.1413,Hon. Mr. TARTE.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"In my opinion, my hou. friends on the treasury benches make a mistake in not paying suitable salaries. A minister of the Crown is not paid enough, though it is true he has the honour of leading a great party, and he has the privilege of being a Privy Councillor. But if you want, in this age, to get good men, honest men, you must pay them well. In my humble opinion the president of such a commission as this should be as well paid as the manager of a great railway corporation. I take the liberty of throwing out the suggestion, which perhaps may come more fittingly from me as I am an independent member of the House. The' government might perhaps on this occasion, at any rate, pay some consideration to the advice which I am tendering, and which I believe will be echoed by those who have given this subject some attention. The salary of $10,000 is altogether inadequate. The government will not be able to get a strong man as president of this commission for any such salary.

,Liberal,,Joseph Israël Tarte,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a1231855-4bec-419e-9184-2deabd03d8a5&Language=E&Section=ALL
88130,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.15,1903-08-06,06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9,ca.m.931,Mr. MACLEAN.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"I would like to see the chief commissioner mentioned in this resolution paid at least $15,000 a year, and the two other commissioners paid $10,000. I would also like to see the manager of the government railways in this country paid at least a salary of $15,000. You canuot get men of the calibre required to take these offices, I believe, for a less sum than $15,000. Men who discharge similar duties in other positions are in receipt of $25,000 a year, and some of larger sums. Some bank managers are getting $15,000 to $20,000 a year, men who are not required to perform duties so important as those which men in this position will have to perform. 1 am not afraid to say in this House that 1 think the time has come when parliament ought to revise the salary list, and pay men of high executive capacity, and they are very rare, substantial salaries, something
like what they would get in the open market when other great corporations required to choose executive officers.

,Independent Conservative,,William Findlay Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9&Language=E&Section=ALL
88131,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.10.16,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",BRITISH CABLE NEWS SERVICE.,,"My own inclination would run in the direction indicated by the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean). There was a time when my ideas of economy were perhaps different from what they are today. At one time I thought it possible to diminish our public expenditure by millions of dollars. But I notice lately that every time we have attempted to do that our friends on the other side have prevented us from doing it. Therefore, 1 do not know exactly what to do in this matter, so I have taken the safe course of suggesting that we should adopt a salary of $10,000 a year. 88218,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.72,1903-08-06,0584c1e1-b6cf-4b4b-bb53-943e8168b396,ca.m.1581,Mr. CLARKE.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"Of course, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier pointed out how these men could be imposed upon, and if the desire of parliament is to protect them and to see that they are paid the current rate of wages, we ought to be able to provide machinery to carry out our intention.

88223,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.77,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"These fair-wage officers who are in existence may be used for the purpose of giving advice to the Minister of Railways and Canals when he is called upon to decide as to whether or not a contractor is complying with the terms of his contract, but I think it would be going rathefr too far to say that we should substitute a fair-wage officer for the minister in connection with an important matter of this sort.

88224,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.78,1903-08-06,d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68,ca.m.2854,Mr. MONK.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I think with some other hon. gentlemen that it is very important if it is possible that we should protect the workingmen, because there is no doubt-I say this with no desire to appear as the protector of the workingman especially-that they will be the sufferers unless some relief can be afforded to them by the amendment suggested by my hon. friend. When this session opened, the hon. Minister of Justice will remember that I had a Bill before the House by which I endeavoured to place the responsibility for fires caused by railway companies upon the railway companies, but I admitted that the matter of torts or damages was a provincial matter and that we

could not directly legislate in this House that railways under the control of this Dominion should be responsible for fires caused by their locomotives. I thought that was impossible because it was an invasion of the provincial field by the Dominion legislature. Therefore, my Bill consisted of an endeavour to make clearer some provisions of the Interpretation Act so as to arrive indirectly at the result which it was desired to obtain. But that did not meet with the views of the hon. Minister of Justice ; whereas, a direct law decreeing in very words that the railway companies shall be responsible for fires caused by the locomotives, is now incorporated, as I understand, in this Bill. In other words if my view is correct we have legislated on a matter of damage and tort which is in the provincial field exclusively in a manner designed to meet the point. According to the view entertained by my hon. friend, I suppose that we were legislating in regard to Dominion railways and that therefore we could impose any conditions that we chose upon the railways under our control even if those conditions constituted an invasion of the provincial field of legislation. I believe that has been held by the Privy Council in the case of the taxation of the banks which came up before the provincial court and went to the Privy Council. If we can do that why cannot we legislate in the sense that no contract by which a labourer will have contracted out of the conditions mentioned i:n the law will be available before the department, or some such legislative disposition without decreeing especially that any contract made by the labourer with the employer shall be null and void, which might, as the hon. Minister of Justice says, be beyond the powers of this legislature, or say, as least, that any such contract cannot he invoked between the contractor and the labourer in so far as the subsidy granted by this parliament is concerned ? I would not undertake to word the clause ; I have no doubt my hon. friend the Minister of Justice can do it much better than I can. But if we have legislated that the damages occasioned by fires caused by locomotives under the control of railways that are under our control, shall be paid by the railway company, surely we have the right to legislate in regard to the contracts existing between contractors and labourers on railways which are under our immediate control. That is the point I wish to make.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Frederick Debartzch Monk,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68&Language=E&Section=ALL
88225,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.79,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I do not think the two things can be compared. In the case of damage by fires the position is that where an individual who suffers damage applies to the railway company for redress, he can only apply on the principle that there has been fault on the part of the railway company, which fault has resulted in damage to the individual who seeks redress. Wliat the Privy Council decided in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway was, that if a company does that

which the legislature authorized it to do, there can be no fault, and it seems .to me that notwithstanding all that has been said about that judgment, it is a most elementary principle that there can be no fault where there is legislative sanction for doing the thing complained of. With respect to the amendment to which my hon. friend referred, what we decided here was purely and simply that while we authorized the company to operate its road in a particular way-if we limited ourselves to that we would relieve them from responsibility for anything that might happen so long as they remained within the law-we specifically extended that feature in the doing of the thing we authorized, by saying that for damage occasioned by way of fire caused by them, they would be responsible. . That is to say, we limit the extent to which they , would have the right to go in connection with the operation of their road. That is completely within our control. But what I cannot up to the present time see is,where we can get authority to interfere with a contract entered into between two individuals within the limits of any particular province with respect to the lease and hire of service. A contract is made between two individuals, and if the law of a particular province allows absolute freedom of contract with respect to that, then how could we do anything here which could in any way influence that particular contract or modify it ? How can we restrict the right of the parties to that contract? How can we determine any limit to the area within which they can contract ? Where do we get authority to do it ? I Contend that we have a perfect right to say to a man who asks us for assistance, that in consideration of the assistance we are giving him he shall do so and so, and if he doesn't do it we have recourse against him for failure on his part to comply with the terms of his contract. But that wie can govern the relations between himself and some one else for the benefit of that other person, I cannot see where we can get authority to do it.

,,,The MINISTER OF JUSTICE.,

88249,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.103,1903-08-06,92e3635d-9ed3-458d-bc31-944055399f00,ca.m.7386,Mr. KENDALL.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"By clause 211, provision is made to compel all trains to be equipped with certain safety appliances, but by section 212 power is given to the board to exempt railway companies from this obligation. 88259,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.113,1903-08-06,92e3635d-9ed3-458d-bc31-944055399f00,ca.m.7386,Mr. KENDALL.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"If the hon. gentleman will read clause 212, he will see that the railway board is given the power to decide whether these safety improvements shall be applied at all.

,Liberal,,Arthur Samuel Kendall,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=92e3635d-9ed3-458d-bc31-944055399f00&Language=E&Section=ALL
88260,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.114,1903-08-06,ca1d8584-67fd-45ae-8abf-9dbac268e505,ca.m.5015,Mr. LANCASTER.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I am personally in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall), because it strikes me-as this discussion goes on I may be further enlightened-that section 212 is in exact conflict with section 211, and almost renders nugatory its provisions. We have spent a great deal of time in providing that certain things shall be done for the protection of the men working on the cars and for the protection of travellers also. Section 211 declares what shall be done and what appliances shall be provided. As I understand the amendment of the hon. member for Cape Breton, it is not what the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). supposed, but it is of a. character that that hon. gentleman would favour. The amendment simply proposes that the board may have the power to extend the time for providing these appliances, if it thinks right to do so. But the section as it stands will give the board power practically to repeal section 211. I am opposed to that. Parliament, in section 211, declares that certain things are necessary for the safety of the public, of the railway employees and of passengers. That is for parliament to say. But, under section 212, the board may say that their opinion is better than ours, and so they may ' exempt the company from using upon its railway or any portion thereof, any of the appliances in the last preceding section mentioned, and may from time to time extend the period with which such appliances shall be used.' I do not think

that it should be for this board, with the I manifold duties that they have to perform, J to undertake the duties of parliament also, ' as they would be authorized to do under this section 212. I think the amendment should carry, because if it does not, we endow the board with power to enact the very opposite of what parliament has enacted.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Edward Arthur Lancaster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ca1d8584-67fd-45ae-8abf-9dbac268e505&Language=E&Section=ALL

time to time extend the period within which such appliances shall be used '-that is, they do not want to be unreasonable in the matter. 88319,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.173,1903-08-06,a8b2b613-dd5c-4a22-8f22-c0e4f180c7b6,ca.m.4552,Mr. GUTHRIE.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I move that the committee reconsider section 242. My object is to move an amendment to section 242. The amendment I intend moving is to add the following as subsection four

Notwithstanding anything in any public or special Act heretofore passed, or in the rules or by-laws of any railway company, or in the rules or by-laws of any insurance or provident society or association of railway employees formed under the authority of any Act heretofore passed, no contract or agreement made or entered into by a workman, employee or servant of any railway company, and no rule or by-law of any society or association as aforesaid. shall be a bar or constitute any defence to an action against such railway company by such workman, employee or servant, for the recovery of compensation or damages for personal injury to him, or, in case the injury results in death, to an action by the personal representatives of such workman, employee or servant-

(a.) unless for such workman, employee or servant entering into such contract or agreement, or becoming a member of such insurance or provident society, there was other consideration than that of his being taken into, or continued in the employment of the railway company ;
(b.) unless such other consideration is, in the opinion of the court or judge before whom such action is tried, ample and adequate ; nor
fc.) unless, in the opinion of the court or judge, such contract or agreement, in view of

su'ch other consideration, was not on the part of the workman, employee or servant, improvident, but was just and reasonable ; and the burden of proof with respect to such other consideration, and of its being ample and adequate, and that the contract was just and reasonable, and was not improvident, shall in all cases rest upon the railway company.
That clause is taken from the Ontario Act known as the Workmen's Compensation Act. A similar Act is in force in several of the other provinces. The difficulty I seek to remedy is this :
column2: Some railway companies, by means of special legislation or special clauses incorporated in their charter, have been able to form insurance or provident society, and by means of a summary contribution to the funds of these societies, they are able to have a great deal to say in their management and the formation of rules to govern them. In the case of one of these companies, the Grand Trunk Railway, which employs about 25,000 men, it has formed such a society, under the authority of an Act passed by this parliament in 1874, and amended in 1878, giving it power to form a provident society and conduct the business of accident and life insurance. No one objects to their doing so, hut the difficulty is that provision is made in the rules of the society for the immunity of the railway company, on the payment of a small fee per head according to the number of members, from every liability in the case of accident. In the Grand Trunk Railway provident society, there is a rule to this effect, rule number 15, which reads as follows :

column1: In consideration of the subscription of the Grand Trunk Railway to the society, no member thereof or his representative shall have any claim upon the company for compensation on account of injury or deaths from accident.

The men are charged fairly high rates for the small insurance they get. They are charged 50, CO, 75 and 80 cents per month for an insurance, which in many cases is only $250. The. premium is much higher than is charged for a much larger amount of insurance in other benevolent and friendly institutions. It has been proved in a court of law that benefit associations doing business in Ontario to-day, give, for a lower rate, insurance of a thousand dollars, instead of $250, and the same weekly benefits in the case of sickness or injury. For many years this rule lay dormant. The Grand Trunk Railway never set it up in an action for damages, but in later years it has been set up in such actions almost invariably. In Ontario the only decision we have by a judge of tbe Superior Court is the decision of the trial judge in the case of Holden against the'Grand Trunk Railway, which was tried at Hamilton. In that case the Grand Trunk Railway set up rule fifteen as a defence for the action, and the trial judge upheld the defence. That case went to the court of appeals, but unfortunately it was not there decided on the point I hav# men-

tioned, but the decision of the court was based on the question of contributory negligence. It has been decided, however, in the Superior Court in the case of Grenier against the Queen-a case arising out of an accident on the Intercolonial Railway where a similar rule is in force-that that rule is binding on the workman and his representatives.

Now, this is in direct antagonism to all modern legislation on the subject of master and servant. Other corporations, large enl-ployers of labour, are bound by the Workmen's Compensation Act in Ontario and similar Acts in other provinces. They cannot escape their common law liability, unless they do so on the giving of some consideration other than the fact of the employment. If they wish to secure themselves, it is open to them to take out accident policies in the various insurance companies doing that line of business. So, I submit, it should be with the Grand Trunk Railway Company or other companies having such a rule as this. Now, it has been stated that this amendment in a manner deals with the question of civil rights, which is ultra vires of this parliament. But, I think that proposition may well be doubted. The only decision we have upon the subject has upheld it. The Ontario law was pleaded in the case of Holden vs. The Grand Trunk, but the trial judge said : No, the rule is binding ; it is passed under the authority of Dominion legislation in 1874 and 1878 ; the Grand Trunk Railway Company is a Dominion corporation. And so the rule was upheld, notwithstanding the Workmen's Compensation Act in the province of Ontario. Now, I submit that no harm can be done to any one by engrafting that legislation upon the Dominion statutes. It will be a long time before a railroad workman who has lost an arm or a leg, or before the widow of a railroad workman who has been killed in an accident on the road, can go to the court of Appeal or the Privy Council to find out whether that statute in Ontario is binding upon the railroad companies or not. You can remove all doubts by placing that legislation in the Dominion Railway Act. I bring it up here because the Bill that I introduced early in the session, though it was read a first and a second time and passed the Railway Committee almost unanimously, is very little likely to be reached this session. But, as it was a Bill to amend the Railway Act, I think this is the proper pdace, if it becomes law, to introduce it in the Railway Act as an amendment to section 242. These are briefly the facts, and I would ask leave to reconsider that section with a view to introducing that amendment to subsection 4.

88334,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.188,1903-08-06,57ed8b95-0f38-4d6d-9502-1000823660c3,ca.m.1041,Mr. INGRAM.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I understood the hon. member for Wellington to say that the last Act affecting this case was passed in 187S. I know that under the law of the province of Ontario, an Act was passed excluding the Grand Trunk Railway Company from the operation of the Workmen's Compensation for Injuries Act, by reason of the Grand Trunk Railway Company having an insurance and provident society for their railway employees. A strong fight occurred in the legislature in 1887. The, Grand Trunk Railway took the ground that its employees preferred the benefits of the insurance society rather than the benefits of the Compensation for Injuries Act. As a result of the fight between the employees and the company, the Ontario government issued a lot of questions which they circulated privately to the railway employees of the Grand Trunk Railway asking them whether they would prefer being excluded from the benefits of the Mr. GUTHRIE.

Compensation for Injuries Act and to retain their position in the society ; and I believe over 70 per cent of them answered that while they had no objections to the Provident Insurance Society, at the same time they wanted the benefit of the Compensation for Injuries Act. They said they paid for their insurance, and they felt that they had no right to be deprived of the benefits of the Compensation for Injuries Act. As a result of these answers, the government wiped out the section which excluded the Grand Trunk Railway from the provisions of the Compensation for Injuries Act, and that company came under the provisions of that Act in the province of Ontario. Now I am surprised, to find that the courts are holding that because employees are members of the Provident and Insurance Society they cut themselves out of any benefits that might come to them by reason of the Ontario Compensation for Injuries Act, in case of accident. 88335,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.11.189,1903-08-06,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.","RAILWAY ACT, 1903.",,"I hope the committee will adopt this provision moved by the member for South Wellington. The ex-Minister of Railways says that this is a proposal to alter a special Act. Well, in some respects, probably it is, but I do not understand that the hon. gentleman who proposes the amendment exactly shares in that view, and I do not think it is the fairest way to look at the matter. The ease presented by the hon. gentleman who proposes the amendment is, that it may be quite possible that the special Act granted to a. railway company does not justify the position that the railway company takes, ljut, on the other hand, the railway company does see fit to place upon the Act a certain interpretation, and that interpretation having been placed pai it by the railway company and the decision of the court, standing as it is in the province of Ontario, it is impossible for any person to get at what may be the true interpretation of the statute until he carries it to the ultimate court of appeal. The hon. gentleman points out that it is important that the class of people who invoke the provision of the law for their benefit in a matter of this kind shall not be handicapped by the difficulty of having to carry their case to the $ourt of appeal ; in other words, that the widow and children of deceased employees of the railway companies are not in a position to fight the railway companies. The hon. member asks not for the repeal of the special Act under which the railway company is operating, but for such an amendment as will, in effect, be a declaration of the rights of the parties. That is what it amounts to. He brings in an amendment declaring that the railway companies shall

not have power to contract themselves out of liability unless the contract is founded upon some new construction, independently of the mere fact of admitting a person to the service of the railway company, because it has been well remarked from my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that no just consideration arises out of the mere circumstance of employment; because it is supposed that the employee gives value for every dollar that he gets from the company. We declare the presumed intention of parliament, when it gave the right to the company to grant insurance and to make insurance regulations, namely : that it should not have the power to contract itself out of liability unless it could show that there is some consideration for the contract beyond the mere matter of admitting the employee into the service of the company. In addition to that the hon. gentleman who introduces the amendment, very properly provides that the contract shall be in force only in so far as it is declared by a judge' who tries the case to be just and reasonable. This is no new system of legislation. It is one that is well recognized in various statutes in the province of Ontario, and I apprehend in the statutes of other provinces as well. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), referred to subsection 3 of section 242s and argues, with his usual force and clearness, that there is probably a sufficient safeguard in this section. I venture, with all deference, to submit that the subsection in no way affects the question. It is not an enabling provision at all. It is a mere negative provision. It provides no remedy. It merely provides that:

No inspection had under this Aeit, and nothing in this Act contained, and nothing done or ordered or omitted to be done or ordered, under or by virtue of the provisions of this Act, shall relieve, or be construed to relieve, any company of or from any liability or responsibility resting upon it by law.

In other words, it leaves the law as it was before. But, if any additional argument is required, I wish to refer the hon. gentleman who has charge of this Bill, at the present time, (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to this fact, to be borne in mind, that although we are dealing with a new statute, we are dealing with an old provision. The same provision appeared word for word in the statute of 1888, the General Railway Act; therefore, this provision was in force at the time these difficulties arose, and at the time these matters were brought before the court. I may say, though this is not a matter of great importance, only as illustrating the position that I take, that I have also had personal experience of the matter. I have not been so unwise, I admit, as to bring an action, under such circumstances, because I realized that unless one has a pot of money it is impossible to follow these railway companies from court to court, but I held a brief in 256

a case which came up for trial at Brampton after the decision in the case of Holden vs. the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the learned judge who was sitting there declined to hear the case. He, of course, gave us a suggestion that it was not wise to press the matter, and in effect told me that he would not try the case until he had heard tlie ultimate result In the case of Holden vs. the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The hon. member who proposes this amendment has explained that that case was not decided in appeal upon this question, but on another point-showing that the judges regarded it as a question of difficulty, and, therefore, they will not decide this question finally by way of appeal until they are driven to it. The fact that it is a matter of difficulty and that it is a questionable point, ought to be sufficient, I submit, to induce this committee, having regard to the necessity, the vital importance it is to the widows and children of a deserving class of our people who are not able to protect themselves in all cases, to accept this amendment. I do not often have the pleasure of supporting an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, but I have great pleasure in doing so upon this occasion.

88393,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.14.1.1,1903-08-06,,,,stagedirection,,,,"At the last meeting of the North-west Assembly that passed an ordinance with reference to this matter, to amend chapter 87 of thie Consolidated Ordinances of 1898, entitled an Ordinance for the Prevention of Prairie and Forset Fires. It says :
Section 21 of the Prairie Fires Ordinance is hereby amended by adding thereto the following subsection :-

(2) If a fire -shall be caused by the escape of sparks or any other matter from any engine or other thing it shall be deemed -to have been kindled by the person in charge or who should be in charge of such engine or other thing, but such person or his employer shall not be liable to the penalties im-p-oised by this section if in the case of stationary engines the precautions required by section 12 have been complied with and there has been no negligence in any other respect or in the oase of railway or other locomotive engines -such engine i-s equipped with a suitable smoke stack netting and ash pan netting in good repair and kept closed and in proper place and in ithe case of railway engines where the line of railway passes through prairie country there is maintained for a distance of at least three miles continuously in each direction from the point at which the fire starts on each side of such line of railway and not less than two hundred nor more than four hundred feet therefrom a good and sufficient fire-guard of ploughed lan-d not less than sixteen f-eeit in width kept free from weed® and other inflammable matter and the space between such fire-guard and such line of railway is kept burned -or .otherwise freed from the danger of spreading fire and there has been no negligen-ce in any other respect.

That is the ordinance, but I think the hon. Minister of Justice will perhaps agree that this will he considered ultra vires, and that it would be disallowed by the government on account of it interfering with matters over which the territorial government had no control. An arrangement was eventually obtained, as mentioned by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), hut not until lie companies became afraid that legislation would be passed here compelling them to do something themselves. The government of the North-west Territories has been offering to assist them in -doing this work for years, hot up to the present time they have not shown any disposition to do their part. My statement is borne out by an extract from a letter which the acting Commissioner of Public Works of the Northwest Territories sent to the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) :

I n-o.te your remarks regarding the possibility that the second reading of your Bill to amend the Bail-way Act regarding fire-guards may not be reached this session. We had, as you know, opened negotiations with the railway company with the object of getting them to be put in proper system of fire-guards before -the Bill was introduced, but had failed to get any satisfaction. Almost immediately after the introduction of your Bill -they telegraphed here for Mr. DAVIS.

further information, and it now looks, from correspondence which the deputy commissioner has had with Superintendent Leonard, as if the company were going to come to time and agree to pu-t in a proper system of fire-guards. I am quite satisfied that the introduction of the Bill caused this matter to move, and even if it has not re-ached its second reading, the fact that such legislation has bee-n introduced a-nd will probably be pressed next session will, without d-oubt. have the effect of making the Canadian Pacific Railway a.nd Canadian Northern Railway deal with this very important question.

Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that the fact that the Bill was introduced by the bon. member for West Assiniboia had the effect of waking them up, and a correspondence was -started on this subject between the superintendent of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Leonard, in Winnipeg, and tlie territorial government, but up to the present time nothing satisfactory has come of it. I have already read a telegram from the territorial government saying that the arrangement that they had with the railway companies was being cancelled, and in connection with that I have read from the acting Commissioner of Public Works of the North-west Territories, giving the reasons why the territorial government have terminated this contract between the railway companies and themselves. He says :

As you are aware, in the spring of 1902 this government took up the question of fire-guard' construction with the Canadian Pacific Railway, owing to the very unsatisfactory manner in which the work had been done-or, in other words, had not been done-in years past, thus rendering a larger area of the Territories liable-to destruction by fire, for want of a proper fireguard along the line. This work is done in the interests of the settlers and not for the benefit of the railway company. A contract was signed in which the company agreed to contribute one-half the cost of construction of fire-guards along their line, up to a maximum of $10 per mile, that is, the railway company would not pay more than $10 per -track mile for a guard on the two sides of the track, or, in other words, a maximum of $5 per mile of guard. For reploughing this guard, the company would only pay one-half the cost of the work, hut in no case would they pay a sum exceeding $2.50 per mile of guard or $5 per mile of track. All the cost of inspection and everything incidental thereto was to be borne by the government, and in addition, in event of the guard having to make a detour around sloughs and other obstructions, the government pays the additional mileage caused thereby. Considerable difficulty was experienced last year in getting persons to tender for the work, and in fact a great many contracts entered into were never completed, or were only done in a most unsatisfactory manner, leaving no guard in some places on either side of the track, in several places only a few furrows, -some here and gome there, so you can easily imagine how inefficient a guard has been made. In many instances we were called upon to pay a higher price than $10 per mile of gmard, but the Canadian Pacific Railway, of course -only paid $5, the department paying the balance, and as I have already stated, bearing the cost and trouble of advertising for tenders, staking out and inspecting the guards.

This year a. very small number of unfinished portions of these guards have been completed in the vicinity of Dunmore and Cowley. From your intimate knowledge of the question, you will know full well that guards constructed last year will require backsetting or other work done on them this year to render them efficient, and safe should we have an abundance of rain, followed by a dry season in August or September.

At the present time, we are using our best endeavours to complete the work begun last year, and re-ploughing or disk-harrowing the portions of the guard finished, so as to render efficient protection to the country along the railway lines from Morley ts Broadview, and along the Crow's Nest and other branches, but owing to the demand for contract work of all classes, we are having difficulty in securing competent men to proceed with the work. We are endeavouring to deal with the guard along the line from Gull lake to Broadview and the Soo branch from the office. Mr. Stocks, assistant chief engineer, is travelling over the western portion of the line and the Crow's Nest line to see what he can do there, and we will probably know in the course of two weeks' time just how the matter stands. ' I may add here, that the work is of that class that should be done by the railway company themselves, they having, or being able to obtain, everything required in connection therewith and having the means of transporting contracting outfits along the line and getting them any supplies, so that it is hoped that your best efforts will be used toward getting a Bill through parliament to compel the railway company to do this work and not leave the matter as it is now, for the government or the people to do to protect themselves against the company. I may add in conclusion that a contract was submitted to the department last year by Messrs. Osier, Hammond & Nanton, on behalf of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway and the C. and E. Railway, upon somewhat the same basis as that entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and was returned to them some time in July, if I remember rightly, for amendment, as they had included the whole line from Prince Albert to Regina, along the Q. L. L. and S. Railway, and from Macleod to Stnathiooma, on tlhe C. and E., whereas lit was only inltemded to make a guard along the Prince Albert branch from Regina to Saskatoon and along the C. and E., from Macleod to Olds. Thinking that the contract would be returned With this amendment, the department proceeded with the work of constructing the guard along the two lines and practically completed a fireguard along both sides of the C. and E. Railway, from Madleod to Olds, and had a small amount of the work done on the Q. L. L. and S. Railway. The contract was never returned, and as a result the government paid for all the work done.

You were informed by the commissioner by telegraph some months ago, that notice had been given to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that the contract had been cancelled. This will take effect on December 31st next. Since that time the Q. L. L. and S. Railway and the C. and E. Railway people have been notified that It is not the intention of the department to undertake any further work of constructiong fireguards along these two lines.
I have also a further letter, dated July 17th, containing additional information,
with special reference to the C. and E. and Q. L. L. and Sask. Companies, as follows :

Since the question of the construction and reploughing of these guards has been taken in hand this year some correspondence has taken place between the department and Messrs. Osier, Hammond & Nanton, who represent these two railway companies, they being now able to produce the contract which was returned to them for execution in July, 1902. They have returned copies of the contract covering the Q. L. L. and S. Railway from Regina to Saskatoon, and the C. and E. Railway from Macleod to Oldis, duly executed. Unfortunately the late commissioner had executed these contracts on behalf of the department before forwarding them to Messrs. Osier, Hammond & Nanton ; dioiulbtless had it been left for the railway companies to perform their part and sign the contract first, these copies would have been returned long since, so you will understand that as far as the records of this office are concerned, the only inference we could draw was, that the C. and E. and the Q. L. L. and S. people had not and did not desire to execute the contracts at the time they were returned to them, last year, owing to the proposed amendments. I may add that these contracts were received by the department only yesterday, July 16th. It perhaps would be saying too much to state that Messrs. Osier, Hammond & Nanton showed had faith in not returning these contracts at the time they were returned to them for execution, but they are cerainly guilty of neglecting performing their part of the contract.

In other words these contracts were signed and sent back after the discussion about fireguards took place in this House. They kept them until they found there was to be legislation here, and then they signed these contracts and sent them back. I do not see why the government of the North-west Territories should he compelled to expend a large sum of money to do work that the railway companies themselves should properly do. It is their engines that set fire to the prairie and do the damage, and they should be compelled to protect the people. I hope that now that this matter is before the House, the Minister of Justice, who has charge of the Bill, will take steps to insert a clause in this Bill that will cover the ground and give power to the commission to see that proper guards are made. I quite understand that difficulty may arise from the fact of railways having to plough outside of their right of way on land that does not belong to them, but any one who is acquainted with the North-west Territories knows that there are miles and miles of government land where they could not be interfering with the rights of any person, and any way no one would object if they ploughed up fire-guards and carried out the idea suggested in tlie amendment. In the amendment which I have submitted, the commission before enforcing this, would have to get authority from the government of Manitoba or the government of the territories.",,,,

88394,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.14.2,1903-08-06,3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149,ca.m.3785,Mr. GOURLEY.,,"QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",G. H. V. BULYEA.,,"I think I have never had an opportunity of agreeing with the mem-

ber for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) since 1 have been in the House, until this evening, and I feel a pleasure in getting in touch with him at last. I know that the Minister of Justice cannot understand the fire-guard question in the slightest degree. No man who has lived in the east, no matter how intelligent he is-and the Minister of Justice I presume has the ordinary intelligence of the men of the east-no man in the east understands the question of fire-guards. A man has to live in the west, and to have experience in the west, before he understands the extraordinary difficulties connected with the fire-guard question. Before I had lived in the North-west long enough to become familiar with this matter, the question of fire-guards would have been utterly meaningless to me, but now, I know that it is a paramount question there. A rancher with 20,000 acres of grazing land, and a large stock of either cattle or sheep, is absolutely dependent upon the preservation of his pasture land for the preservation of his stock. A prairie fire may ruin him in a night. I have seen prairie fires do immense destruction within 24 hours, and within 48 hours in a grazing country that was smiling with green grass, I have seen the verdure disappear, and thousands and thousands of acres burned and browned, and the rancher compelled to take up his location and go hundreds of miles away, at a cost which was enough to ruin him. I recollect one evening, the ranch people having been at work all day gathering hay, suddenly some one saw a few miles away the appearance of a prairie fire. The whole country was alarmed and well it might. I Could not realize what the alarm was about, but in a few hours I saw this tremendous sheet of flame apparently as far as the human eye would carry, racing upon the people's stock, and the whole country side and the Mounted Police turning out and fighting that fire as if it were an invading army. It is a matter of the most vital importance to the rancher, whether he is going to be exposed day after day, and night after night, during the dry season in that country, to this alarming danger. The railway runs through the ranching country for hundreds of miles. A man's property may abut against the railway for ten or fifteen miles, and that whole country is exposed to a single spark setting the prairie fire going, and the man's ranch may be burned down, and thousands of square miles swept clean of a bit of verdure within 24 hours. No man can afford to have a band of sheep, or a bunch of cattle, in that country, without putting up a large quantity of hay for the winter. The winter may be soft and he may not need the hay, but on the other hand he may be compelled to feed his cattle for a considerable time, and then the salvation of the stock depends upon having a quantity of hay safely housedi The danger of a prairie fire is therefore double. It not only clears away the growing grass, Mr. GOURLEY.

but it destroys the hay which the rancher has preserved for the protection of his stock in the winter time. Consequently, the Minister of Justice should reflect upon this problem, as one of vital interest to the people of the North-west. I want it to be understood, that I have no quarrel with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am friendly to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I believe it to be one of the greatest institutions in Canada, and I have never been able to sympathize with the people of the Northwest, who have indulged as I think, in the most unjust and ungenerous criticism of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has done so much to develop their country. When I was in the west, I could not help but notice that the whole development of that west depended largely upon the Canadian Pacific Railway. Of course, when it was a young enterprise, it had to charge rates that were considered in the east high, but that was unavoidable. That was never a sufficient basis for any man to object to, or to abuse the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was a very proper basis, on which to-negotiate with the Canadian Pacific (Railway, and to appeal, for a reduction of their charges, but there was an attempt in certain quarters of the North-west, to arouse popular prejudices against the Canadian Pacific Railway, simply in order to play to the gallery. I always felt that unjust. There were, it is true, rightful criticisms to be levelled against the Canadian Pacific Railway, but these were magnified and distorted beyond reasonable bounds. I am not speaking to-night as an opponent of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I believe, that the Canadian Pacific Railway has been one of the greatest national institutions ever created in Canada, and that, it has done more to give us a national status, than even the distinguished nation maker opposite. At the same time while I do not wish to press anything against the Canadian Pacific Railway,

I think that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be called upon, to do justice in the-matter of fire-guards. I have some small interest in the North-west now, and I am compelled every year to undergo serious pecuniary loss for protecting property against fire. Gentlemen in the east do not know what the ploughing of fire-guards is. You may have a grazing territory there of considerable extent, and twenty or thirty miles away you have what is called a home ranch, where your home and your buildings are. you may drive your flocks or herds thirty miles away to pasture, but there is a home ranch consisting of probably 640 acres, and to protect that home ranch by fire guards, you have to send your men once, or perhaps twice a year to plough around that home ranch, a breadth of 30 or 40 feet, in order to protect your buildings from prairie fires.
If a man's ranching territory happens to lie near the railway, he has to plough for miles along it in order to protect his ranch

from the danger of fire. That burden in my time was thrown entirely on the ranchers, and it is an enormous burden. I have known men to be ploughing day by day and week by week. The furrow is so long that a man who starts in the morning hardly gets it e mpleted by night. 1 have no doubt that the Minister of Justice, from the narrow limits of his experience in the province of Quebec-I mean the mere knowledge of space and distance which no man in the east can have-is unable to realize the idea of magnificent distance which one gets on those magnificent prairies. Unless a man has that idea, he cannot comprehend what enormous burdens are thrown on the man who has great flocks and herds in the west and the immense pastures on which they subsist. A man may to-night be as rich in flocks and herds as Job, and to-morrow he may be as poor as Uazarus. In this case the hon. member for Saskatchewan is absolutely right. He has presented a real grievance, unlike many of the North-west grievances, which are entirely a play to the gallery. It is, a grievance thoroughly well based, and we must not go headlong and place the blame at the wrong door or the expense of rectifying the grievance where it does not belong. With regard to the constitutional difficulty, many men in this House are oppressed with constitutional difficulties. It is time we were done with this provincial rights business. A great deal of that difficulty arose from political questions. Whenever a man, who had not much mind to think or anything to say, wanted to say something, he would get up and talk about provincial rights. No matter how shallow he was, he could talk learnedly about provincial rights. There is no question of provincial rights involved in this case. When this parliament is properly seized of a subject matter which the constitution has vested in it, we can pursue that subject to the end, and no question of civil rights can intervene until parliament has exhausted its power of legislation on the subject matter in question. On this matter, which is a pure matter of railway legislation, we can legislate until we exhaust the subject, even if in doing that we enter the domain of what may be regarded as merely provincial rights; and if after we are done, nothing is left, no person can raise that question. It is of no use for the railway company to have guards inside their fences. The difficulty from fires is always twenty or thirty or forty yards outside the railway fences. The ranchman who ploughs his fire-guards ploughs them thirty or forty yards, or it may be one hundred yards, outside of the railway fence; and if you give him protection you must give it to him there. The land outside the railway fence, as a rule, belongs either to the government or to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If it belongs to the company, there is no harm in forcing the company to plough fire-guards on their own

land outside of the fence. If it belongs to the government, and we give the Canadian Pacific Railway Company power to plough these fire-guards, there can be no harm in that. If it belongs to a ranchman, he will be happy to give the railway company power to go on the land and plough the fire-guards, because if the railway company does not do it, the ranchman will have to do it at his own cost. Whether the railway company should be charged with the whole cost or not is a matter of equity for the Railway Commission to decide. But in any case there should be some provision in this Bill. Whether the provision proposed by the hon. member for Saskatchewan is the right one or not, I do not know, but the mere wording of the Act would be a very simple matter once the principle to govern this thing were settled. It is, a matter of vital importance that this matter should be settled, or some day the whole North-west', along that railway, will be burned up, and a serious injury will be done to the whole stock interest of that country. They have been avoided on many an occasion with the greatest difficulty, and only by the whole country side turning out, and especially because of the good work done by that splendid body, the North-west Mounted Police. I have seen these policemen save the North-west many times from enormous disaster. They have a perfect system for fighting prairie fires. It is wonderful to see that magnificent body attack a prairie fire with military precision and overcome it just as they would an enemy that would venture to assail Canada. I cannot say too much in praise of that fine organization. It is one of the greatest organizations that could exist in any civilized country for the beneficent purposes of civilization. What it accomplishes in favour of good government and the protection of the North-west from lawlessness and destruction of property is beyond the comprehension of the ordinary man in the east. Therefore on all grounds, I would urge the Minister of Justice to take up this question and deal with it. It is the most important I have heard raised in the whole debate, on the Railway Bill. The only trouble is that our friends from the North-west raise many questions and throw such an amount of dust around every question they raise, that it is difficult to say which is the important and strong question to which parliament should turn its attention. This is one of the serious questions which ought to be dealt with in the interests of the ranches of the North-west, and I speak as an eastern man with some knowledge of the subject.

BULYEA.,,"No, the better way appeared to be to authorize the board to require the company to make proper fireguards, but that would not become operative until the local authority had passed the necessary and proper legislation. I understand that there is no doubt at all but that they will pass that legislation, and when they do pass it, then the power conferred on the board, under the 24th section of this Bill, subsection e, will enable it to require the company to provide fireguards. The subsection is as follows :

With respect to the use of any engine, of nettings, screens, graites and other devices, and the use of any engine or car of any appliances and precautions, and, generally in, connection with the railway respecting the const-ruction, use ail'd maintenance of any fire-guard or works which may be deemed by the board necessary and most suitable to prevent as far as possible fires froim being started, or occurring, upon, along, or near the right of way of the railway.

You have there ample power conferred on the hoard to order the construction of fire-guards. My hon. friend ' shakes his head. You have all the power parliament can give the railway hoard to require that these precautions should be taken. It is proposed by the present amendment that this clause shall be inserted :

Provided that in respect of fire-guards the, board may, if empowered to do so, by the leg-isiature of the North-west Territories or the legislature of Manitoba, order the company to enter upon lands nut owned by it, to construct and maintain such fire-guards, and no claim for damages shall be maintained against the company for any act done in compliance with the order of the hoard.

BULYEA.,,"Why the provincial legislature ? We are fully competent. If the hon. gentleman would suggest a legal argument which precludes that competency, I am not so prejudiced as not at once to give in. But I can see nothing in the constitution of Canada to prevent our fully exhausting the subject in every way. We are seized with the power to make an Act on this subject matter. Once seized with the subject matter, we cannot be ousted from that jurisdiction by any claim of the provincial legislature. I think there may have been, at one time, in the early days of the study of the constitution, a narrower idea prevailing; but I am persuaded that this is the correct construction of the constitution, and tile one approved by our constitutional lawyers, by the Privy Council, and by every authority. For instance, it was once the idea, among provincial judges, that this parliament, though It was clothed with power to legislate, fully, upon bankruptcy, it could not invade, or overcome, a provincial Act, that gave a preference. That is exploded to-day. It is now held, that if we undertake to legislate upon bankruptcy, we can exhaust every civil right known to the law, and oust every provincial statute, if necessary, and if we deem it wise policy. Wie can deal with the subject of promissory notes ; we can deal with the subject of execution. Provincial laws may give priority in execution. We can come in, and destroy in a moment; no control by the provincial legislatures, over matters of property and civil rights can stand in our way. In these matters the provincial control over questions of property and civil rights means control of what is left after we have done legislating on the subject. That is to say, if we undertake to legislate, with regard to property and civil rights, on a subject over which we have jurisdiction, there is nothing

for the provincial legislatures except what is left outside of our legislation. This parliament has vested in it the right to legislate on the subject of railways. We can regulate them, control them, confer powers upon them, and require them to exercise those powers in a certain way. When we enter upon that subject, we can exhaust every civil right, and we have no right to make our legislation depend upon anything done or left undone by a provincial legislature. That is why, in the Railway Committee, I urged that every mile of railway should be declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, in order that we might have one law, one set of rules governing all the railways in the country. Therefore,

I would like to hear the Minister of Railways and Canals state specifically, if there is any reason why we should not provide that every railway shall, within two hundred or five hundred yards of its own fences, and of its own right of way, make a fire-guard, and then, having made that general order, provide wise regulations for carrying it out. Take the case of Dominion property. We could provide that the company shall have the right to go upon that land without compensation. Our Act would be a license to any railway company. This would provide for fire-guards on the property that belongs to the Dominion. Then, with reference to the property that belongs to the Canadian Pacific Railway-and every other lot along the railway, that has not been sold belongs to them-no question would arise, because they would have the right to make fire-guards across their own property. There might be another class of lands, those belonging to private individuals. The owners would be only too happy to agree to the employees of the company going upon their land to plough a fire-guard. In my own case I would be only too happy to welcome them. In the case of these lands we can make some provisions that, if the Canadian Pacific Railway offered to make the fire-guard over private lands and the right to do so was refused, that should be a perfect defence in any suit for damages that might arise. I think that would be perfectly fair. So, for these three classes of land-government land. Canadian Pacific Railway land and land of private individuals-we could make regulations here that would be perfectly constitutional, and against which there could be no objections. I do not think it is right for us to be constantly deferring to the supposed rights of provincial legislatures, making our legislation depend upon those supposed rights when really there are no such rights in existence.

BULYEA.,,"I rose this afternoon to ask the minister to allow the committee to return to section 242, which deals with actions for damages. I think the present clause does not cover the point

The freight train was loaded with cattle, and the men were asleep in the caboose. At midnight another freight train came along, ran into the cattle train, and these three men were killed. Of course, an inquiry was made into the cause of the accident. An inquest was held on one of the men who was killed, but the coroner did not take much pains to probe the facts. It seems that he was very anxious to get through with the inquest, and a full inquiry was not made. He refused to allow the solicitors for the friends of the men who were killed to examine witnesses. A verdict was given and all parties seem to have been exonerated from blame. My reason for bringing this matter up is that I think something should be placed in this Bill to protect men who entrust their lives and their property to the hands of the railway companies. Of course, accidents may occur, but whenever the railway employees or the company are to blame for the accident, these men should have redress, and I hope that the hon. Minister of Justice will see his way clear, now that this has been explained, to place a clause in this Bill covering the case. Held, that the condition was valid and could be taken advantage of by the connecting railway company, who therefore were not liable to the shipper for injuries suffered by him in a collision caused by their servants' negligence.
The judge says :

By the contract between the plaintiff and the Bay of Quinte Company, it was provided, by the terms of the 17th clause of the agreement endorsed upon the receipt note, that ' When free passes are given to persons in charge of animals, it is only on the express condition/that the railway company are not responsible for any negligence, default, or misconduct of any kind, on the part of the company or their servants, or of any other person or persons whomsoever, causing or tending to cause the death, injury or detention of any person or persons travelling upon any such free passes, and whether such free passes are used in travelling on any regular passenger train, or on any other train whatsoever ; the person using any such pass takes all risks of every kind, no matter how caused.
It will be observed that this clause merely exempts the contracting company from liability and does not refer at all to the defendant company.
The judge comments on that clause in this way :

The fact that he was being carried free, if it was a fact, would make no difference, as appears from the Jennings case. But I do not think there is any evidence that he was being carried free. I should find, as a fact, that the consideration that he paid for the carriage of the cattle included his own carriage or the carriage of some person in charge of the cattle. For, by clause seventeen, above referred to, it was necessary for the plaintiff himself, or some one under his direction, to travel with the cattle to take charge of them, as will appear from the directions therein contained (the learned judge read clause 17 and continued) :

It is perfectly manifest, I think, and I should find as a fact that the cattle would not have been delivered for the purpose of carriage had not the company agreed to some one going along with them for the purpose of looking after them. It was as much a part of the contract that the plaintiff, or some one In his hehalf, should go with the cattle, as it was that the cattle should be carried by the company.
I do not see anything to exonerate the defendant from liability.

That was the decision in the case. The jury found $5,000 damages against the company for causing the injury to this man, but on appeal, judges Osier, MacLen-nan, Lister and Moss, all disagreed with Judge Rose, the trial judge in the case. The judgment in appeal was unanimous, but it shows that the law is not by any means very clear.

BULYEA.,,"This parliament now enacts that when stock gets injured on a railway by reason of the negligence of the railway company, the company shall be responsible, and it strikes me as the most remarkable thing that a man can contract himself out of any compensation because of accident, when in nine cases out of ten he never reads the contract, and only accepts the pass and signs the contract under the impression that he cannot ship his cattle unless he accompanies them or lias a caretaker to do so. Why should the caretaker of cattle on a train be able to contract himself, and his family in case of his death, out of the possibility of securing damages because of the negligence of the railway company ? It does not seem fair to me as a layman. They compel the caretaker to go with the cattle, and if he accepts a pass then he contracts himself out of any liability on the part of the railway company. There are suits arising from this accident that occurred at Galt, and there is no question at all but that it was due to the gross carelessness on the part of a railway employee. The company have a semaphore there, and they have provided everything necessary, if the employees carry out the instructions of the company to prevent accidents, but this accident occurred because of negligence on the part of an employee, and these three men lost their lives and others were injured. It is a hardship to the families of these three men that they have to suffer on account of the loss of their bread winners, and I hope something will be done by the Minister of Justice to remedy this defect in the law.

,Liberal-Conservative,,Andrew B. Ingram,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=57ed8b95-0f38-4d6d-9502-1000823660c3&Language=E&Section=ALL

BULYEA.,,"1 draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact, that while under the law a railway company is supposed not to he able to contract itself out of negligence, at the same time the railway company compels a shipper in certain cases to sign a contract in consideration of a reduced rate to limit the liability of the company. I have a case in mind which no doubt the legal gentlemen in the House are quite familiar with. It is the case of Robinson vs. the Grand Trunk Railway. The race horse ' Henry R.' was injured in a collision, being shipped from the city of St. Catharines. At the time of shipment Robinson was compelled by the railway company to sign a contract, that in consideration of the reduced rate charged by the railway company their liability was limited to $100 in the event of damage through the negligence of the railway. The horse was killed in a collision. An action was brought and the value of the horse was fixed by a St. Catharines jury at $5,000. It turned out upon the trial that although it was stipulated in the contract signed by the shipper, that it was in consideration of a reduced rate, as a matter of fact it was the usual rate charged by that railway, as well as others, and was not a reduced rate.

In appeal, tlie Supreme Court held, following the Vogel case, that while the railway could not contract itself out of negligence, at the same time a man could enter into a contract with a railway company, and in that contract the railway could limit its liability to a specific amount notwithstanding its negligeuce, and that the contract was good although it was not' a reduced rate that was charged as the contract stated. It does seem to me that there ought to be some provision in this Bill to meet an emergency of that kind. I do not think that a railway company should be able to contract against its own negligence in any ease wherever a fare is charged.

BULYEA.,,"The Minister of Justice, not being familiar with the shipping of cattle, did not grasp the full significance of the objection that was raised by Mr. .Robinson, and included in his amendment. It may not have been expressed scientifically, but he was really endeavouring to cure a wrong. In the west, every shipper has to send a caretaker with the cattle, and while the caretaker may technically get a pass, as a matter of fact, he travels in consideration of the charge that is made for the cattle, and Judge Rose was perfectly right in holding that was the true construction of the contract. A part of the money that is paid by the shipper, is paid as much for the transportation of the caretaker, as the transportation of the cattle, but, of course, there can be no opinion among legal men, but, that the court of appeal were perfectly right in holding as they did.

88436,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.14.44,1903-08-06,3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149,ca.m.3785,Mr. GOURLEY.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",G. H. V. BULYEA.,,"I hold that Judge Rose was right and the court of appeal was right, because their decisions were on different points. Now, the question arises, will this parliament sanction any railway company contracting with people to carry their freight, and at the same time contracting that in case the company kill an individual who accompanies the freight, they shall not be responsible to any one for damages ? That is the question before us. The court of appeal has decided that that contract is valid ; but I think that Judge Rose stated the equity of the thing, which should control our action. We are here not to construe hard and fast statutes, but we are here to settle a principle ; and I agree with the hon. member opposite that we should affirm the principle that no railway company should compel anybody to contract that if the company negligently kill an individual there should be no remedy. Up to this time it may have been legal ; but the question is, shall we in future allow the Grand Trunk or any other company to compel a man to sign a contract like that, so that there will be no damages to be paid by the 257

company in case he is killed ? I say that it is not right, and that some remedy should be provided. In the case cited with regard to the horse, the simple point on which that case w^as decided was that both parties had agreed what the damage should be in the case of loss ; and the principle is clear that when a man agrees what his damage shall be, no court can interfere. In that case the shipper need not have shipped the goods until he had made a satisfactory contract ; but having done it, there was no remedy, and I do not see very well how that can be changed. But in the case brought up by the hon. member for Elgin, all we have to do is to provide that no company shall compel any man to forego his right to damage if the damage is caused by negligence of the company, notwithstanding his having used a free pass. I would go that far, because the court would be met by this free pass, and the courts might not all be like Judge Rose, who held that the free pass was not a free pass, but was the holder's right and was part of the contract to carry the cattle. Therefore, I -would provide that no such contract would be valid, and that the conditions on that pass were unreasonable and void. That would cure the whole difficulty. The company would not be allowed to plead those conditions, and the relatives of the party killed would be thrown back upon their remedy at common law without this technical defence of the company. I think the House should say that the man who goes with the cattle should have the protection of the common law. Is it not an awful thing for this parliament to say that the relatives of a man who has been killed have no remedy? I think we should not be put in that position. I think the time has come when we should make a law which would suit another state of affairs, and when those decisions should not longer continue to be made, and they must be made unless we alter the law.

That it is expedient to repeal chapter eight of the statutes of 1901, intituled : ' An Act to provide for the payment of bounties on lead refined in Canada,' and to enact as follows

column2: The Governor in Council may authorize the payment of a bounty of seventy-five cents per one hundred pounds on lead contained in leadbearing ores mined in Canada ; such bounty to be paid to the producer or vendor of such ores, upon evidence that such ores have been smelted in Canada. Provided, that the sum to be paid as such bounty shall not exceed five hundred thousand dollars in any fiscal year. Provided, also, that when it appears to the satisfaction of the minister charged with the administration of this Act that the standard price of pig-lead in London, England, exceeds twelve pounds ten shillings sterling per ton of two thousand two hundred and forty pounds, such bounty shall be reduced proportionately by the amount of such excess.

Payment of the said bounty may be made from time to time to the extent of sixty per centum of the full bounty authorized, subject to adjustment at the close of each fiscal year. If at the close of any year It shall appear that during the year the quantity of lead produced, on which the bounty is authorized, exceeds thirty-three thousand three hundred and thirty-three tons of twio thousand pounds, the rate of bounty shall be reduced to such sum as will bring the payments for the year within the limit mentioned in section one.

If at any time it shall appear to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that 'the charges for transportation and treatment of lead ores in Canada are excessive, or that there is any discrimination which prevents the smelting of such ores In Canada on fair and reasonable terms, (he Governor in Council may authorize the payment of bounty at such reduced rate as may be deemed just, on the lead contained in such ores mined in Canada and exported for treatment abroad.
The said bounties shall cease and determine on the thirtieth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and eight
The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the intention of this Act.-The Minister of Finance.",,,,
