88468,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.16.25,1903-08-06,5e8a24b4-f155-4f3d-aacc-e6da13c93756,ca.m.4254,Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",LEAD BOUNTIES.,,"Then, is the bounty expected to have the result of giving the Canadian market to the Canadian producers to any greater extent than at present? In the next place, will the bounty have the effect, that we all desire, of establishing in this country any of the industries allied to the production of lead-for example, works for the corrosion-I think that is the expression-of lead, and other industries, which, I believe, might be expected to result from the encouragement of this industry by a protective duty ? I do not know whether the Minister of Finance has any information for the House Hon. Mr. FIELDING.

on these subjects; but it seems to me that it would be extremely desirable that some policy of encouragement to the lead-mining industry should be adopted which would bring about results of this kind. If this bounty will not give to the lead producers of British Columbia the control of the home market to any greater extent than they have control at the present time, it will amount, in a great measure, to a bounty on export. If the lead producers have to send to a foreign market for sale all the lead they produce in excess of the 3,000 or 4.000 tons sold in Canada, practically we are paying a bounty to encourage production first, but, in the second place, to encourage the export of what we produce.

Now, I am desirous of supporting the government in any measure which will have the effect of developing this industry in British Columbia and of increasing the production of our own lead mines in Canada, but I would rather see that accomplished in a way which would give the lead producers of this country control of their own market. I dare say, that if it were attempted by means of a revision of the customs duties, it would be necessary to make changes in the customs duties for the purpose of increasing the protection to other industries, but would it not be desirable to do that if by doing so you could not only give the Canadian producers of lead control of the Canadian market, but at the same time give encouragement to the establishment in this country of the other industries to which I have referred ? I have no doubt that all these matters have been under the consideration of the hon. Minister of Finance, but I think it would be well that he should give some information to the committee on this point, because I think he will agree with the rest of us, that if it is possible to accomplish the results which I have indicated, it is desirable to do so. I have a good deal of doubt, myself, as to whether the system of bounties which is proposed by these resolutions would accomplish the result in anything like the way it could be accomplished by increased protection in the shape of customs duties. At the same time, I realize to so very great an extent the importance of this industry, not only to British Columbia, but to the country as a whole, that I am willing to support the government even in this measure which the hon. Minister of Finance has introduced, although I am of the opinion, which I think is very well founded, that a better result might have been accomplished in the way I have indicated. ,Conservative (1867-1942),,Robert Laird Borden,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5e8a24b4-f155-4f3d-aacc-e6da13c93756&Language=E&Section=ALL
88469,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.16.26,1903-08-06,intervention,,,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",LEAD BOUNTIES.,,"It is very largely due to the attitude of the American trusts and combinations, which have practically shut our lead out of the market. As to the general question as to the effect of this bounty upon the home market, I think

ray hon. friend will agree with me that the home market is entirely a question of price. If the producer of lead in British Columbia can sell his lead low enough, he will have control of the home market. This bounty will enable him to sell his lead at a lower rate than he otherwise could sell it for, and in that way he can get access to the market. I do not think the lead producers contemplate dealing in this way with the export trade. They will have to export some, because the total consumption is only 14,000 or 15,000 tons, and they contemplate an output of at least double that, and some portion will have to be exported ; but I anticipate they will supply a much larger amount to the home market than has been done in foi

mer years. 88470,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.16.27,1903-08-06,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",LEAD BOUNTIES.,,"It seems to me that the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) would have done better, if he had followed the advice given by the legislative assembly of British Columbia. They say :

That it is desirable in the interest of silver-lead mining and smelting industries of British Columbia, that the duties on pig-lead and the products thereof imposed by the Dominion of Canada should be so increased as to protect the capital invested in these industries.

That is to say, that these duties should be so increased as to shut out American lead which is being used in Canada, and provide at least a home market for the Canadian producer. Their judgment was that customs duties would have accomplished that better than bounties would, and I think they would have done so. The hon. minister says that if we pay them a bounty and that bounty enables them to sell their lead cheaper so as to compete with the Americans, they will have control of the home market, but would it not be better to put on a customs duty so as to shut out the American lead, and if necessary, in addition to that to grant a small bounty and encourage the manufacture of lead at home. If the government have ignored the recommendation of the legislative assembly, I would have thought that they would have had some regard for the recommendation of the Rossland Liberal Association, which passed a very strong resolution on January 10, 1903, on the same lines. The following resolution was adopted
That we. the members of the Liberal Association of Rossland, do heartily endorse the action of the silver-lead miners and do especially urge upon the Dominion government

the establishment of such duties as will 'secure for Canadian mines the benefits of the entire home market and will enable resumption of work in the many mining districts of British Columbia which are now suffering from great depression.

The government had the recommendation of the legislative assembly, and to make it stronger, the Liberal Association of Ross-la.nd backed it up with their recommendation. I would have expected that the government would have paid a good deal more attention to that, coming, as it does, from their own friends, and their own friends only, than if it had come from another source. But I regret that they have seen fit to ignore the recommendation, and that, instead of increasing the duty, as has been advised by both of these bodies, they propose to give a bounty that will allow the Americans to control our market still which ought to be supplied by our own people at home. In my judgment, the government are not adopting tlie best way to do for the lead miners what they desire. They are not securing the home market to the lead miners of Canada, and while I think they will improve it a little, they would have helped the lead miners much more if they had adopted the advice of their own friends of the Liberal association and had increased the duty so as to secure the home market for our own people.

Suppose we had put some moderate and reasonable customs duty on these articles greater than we now have, these duties would only operate as a protection to the extent of the quantity consumed in the home market, which is about 14,000 tons. The bounty will apply to the output of 33,000 tons, and therefore the benefit of the bounty covers a larger output. I can imagine that even a man who is a protectionist may perhaps see that the bounty system, for the present at all events, might help him better than customs duties. Secretary.
Rossland, B.C., January 10, 1903.
Sir.-I have the honour to inform you that at a largely attended meeting of this association held last night the following resolution was adopted :-

Whereas since the present Canadian tariff was framed, changed conditions have placed Canada in a position to more than supply the lead necessary for home consumption and her mines are now. through the smelters marketing the bulk of their lead product in China, Japan and Europe, while German lead and Mexican lead manufactured in the United States is being marketed in Canada, supplying the most of the demand, to the detriment of the mines, smelters and refineries in Canada ;

Whereas practically all the silver-lead mines are closed, due to the decline in the world's price for silver and lead, in consequence of which the vast amount of money invested in the development of these districts is now lying idle, and workmen, whose wages were as high as any in the United States and higher than the average paid in Missouri, Mexico and Australia are unemployed, and
Whereas the Dominion government has, through some of its members, stated that tariff revision would be made when changed conditions justified it, therefore,

Be it resolved that we, the members of the Liberal Association of Rossland, do heartily endorse the action of the silver-lead miners and do especially urge upon the Dominion government the establishment of such duties as will secure for Canadian mines the benefits of the entire home market and will enable resumption ot work in the many mining districts of British Mr. GALLIHER,
Columbia which are now suffering from great depression.
Be it further resolved that copies of these resolutions be immediately forwarded to the members of the Cabinet, Senate and House of Commons.

Outlook Much Brighter.

Prospects of good times in the silver-lead camps of the Kooitenays have greatly brightened since the assurance has come from Ottawa that the Dominion government will give aid to the producers in the sum of $500,000 a year. From all sections where lead mines are being developed, words of cheer are heard, and there is no doubt that mines which have in recent years been opera ted only in the development stage, will in a short time be thrown open and ore turned out at their full capacity.

Senator Turner, principal owner of the Sullivan group, in East Kootenay, is credited with saying to the Cranbroolc ' Herald ': * The proposed bonus will enable Sullivan Company to start mine immediately and bo complete the smelter this season,'

'As long as the bonus lasts, we may consider that we will have good times for the following reasons :
1st. The mines that are in a shipping condition. but which are not shipping, will naturally ship their ores.
2nd. Those in a developing condition, but not developing, will naturally develop.

3rd. Those properties which have a favourable surface mineral condition, will naturally either have some work done on them, or the owners will find a more favourable market for them than has been the case the past two years.
4th. Encouragement will be given to the prospector to hunt 'for new finds, probably resulting in the later opening up of a new district or two.
5th. The wage expenditure will return to the old standard of about $2,500,000 per annum instead of less than $500,000.
6th. The merchants, who have been reducing their stock, will replenish it, resulting in the merchants east getting fresh orders, and giving the railroads more work.

7th. The smelters will have live furnaces, instead of dead ones, and this will give employment to more men, and through this certain ores available for fluxes can be used and purchased by them which would otherwise have to remain in the ground. LAIRD.,,"I understand that a very important feature in connection with this industry is the supply of fuel. I see that boards of trade and other associations in British Cojumbia have laid great stress on the development of the coal properties owned by the government of Canada in the Crow's Nest Pass. Of course, the intention of the bounty is to place the mining industry of British Columbia on a paying and satisfactory basis as far as possible. Might I ask the government what has been done by them to meet the views of the British Columbia Board of Trade, in which they ask that the government should select their coal lands on Morrissey Creek, and should either develop them as a government work or lease them under such conditions that it would be possible for other mining companies operating in that part of Canada to get control of the output. I made the discovery on a visit to British Columbia last fall that the fuel question there is so important that it is considered that unless it is settled, anything the government can do to foster the lead industry by a bounty might be unavailing. The industry is liable to be interrupted by difficulties in connection with mining by strikes, and would be entirely jeopardized by a serious rise in the price of coal or coke ; so much so that it has been suggested that the government should take steps which would guarantee a sufficient supply of coke or coking coal at a fixed minimum price. I know that this is not related directly to the question of bounties, but, as it is essential that the fuel question be put upon a safe basis before the benefit can be expected

I have not the slightest doubt that the earliest representations made were for duties, but the government are not bound to accede to all the demands that are made upon it. The government are bound to give them a candid hearing, and most courteous treatment, and to weigh the suggestions that are put before them, and having done that in this case, the government have decided to assume the responsibility of the course which they now propose. Therefore, this is aside from the question as to what suggestions were made to the government. The government recognized that the whole country was interested in this industry, and might fairly be called upon to do something to bear part of the burden of encouraging that industry. They have decided that the best way to do that, in their opinion, is in the form of the proposition now before the House. If I were to express an opinion myself in reference to the bonus, I would view it, that probably, when they urged us strongly for duties, they had not anticipated that the government might see its way clear to propose to the House such a large bonus. From the information I can get, strengthened by the telegrams read by the hon. member (Mr. Galliher), it would seem that all parties interested are satisfied. LAIRD.,,"I was surprised to hear the Minister of Customs express himself as he did. He treated this whole question as a matter of expediency ; and as if we should satisfy the people of British Columbia for political reasons only. It would seem from his argument, that the whole object of the policy of the government is to pursue a trimming course in this matter. There is no decided policy on their part as regards free trade or protection, but each one of them seems to be trimming his sails to meet the political exigencies that may arise at the next election. There is a deplorable want of sincerity in the manner in which these gentlemen opposite treat the fiscal policy of this country. The hon. member from Vancouver read a long article from a western paper setting forth how the trade of the country was going to boom on account of the establishment of this bonus, but notwithstanding that, in my opinion the bonus system is entirely wrong. The government is working from the wrong end in this matter, and they are simply trying to postpone the inevitable. We shall have in the end to protect our industries by a legitimate form of protection that will give stability to the industries of the country. You cannot accomplish that, by this hand to mouth proposition of bonusing certain industries. In this country we need a staple fiscal policy that will encourage foreign capital or home capital to invest in legitimate lines. When the government found that we had in the western country a mining industry which needed some protection, the proper thing for the government to do was to give that industry protection in a legitimate form. Instead of that, they give a bonus of $15 a ton which apparently pleases some people, and because it pleases some people the Minister of Customs is perfectly satisfied, and he does not care whether it is taking the money out of the pockets of the people and giving us permanent benefit to the country so long as he thinks it is going to help his political party.

88600,ca.proc.d.1903-08-06.3.18.86,1903-08-06,8ee2f23e-951f-4c93-972d-dc95351fca8c,ca.m.1494,Mr. LEFURGEY.,,QUESTIONS. , CUSTOMS DEPARTMENT SALARIES.",RONALD A. LAIRD.,,"It is pretty long, but it is good and will do the hon. gentleman good. This article is by the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States. He says, speaking against the lowering of the tariff, which was contemplated about that time :
I am only attempting to show the folly of a free trade remedy for an alleged evil.

We are frequently threatened with overproduction. and against this we must always protect by increasing our markets as far as possible. But other countries also have overproduction, and from this source our industries are sure to be crushed unless protected. Does any one suppose any iron industry in the United States could have survived an inundation from Europe occasioned by recent business stagnation in some localities on the continent. but for the tariff.

The Republican party watches primarily that the American labourer shall have employment. It is probable that during the last year or two free trade in iron would have cheapened the product to the American consumer, but a million and a half people, fed and clothed directly by wages paid by the various iron and steel manufactories, would have been again begging bread.

Unreasonable price's are always objectionable. but prices unreasonably low are more objectionable and fraught with greater hardships, primarily to the wage-earner, and, secondly, to all those who supply the wage-earner's necessities, than prices unreasonably high. Do you remember that President Harrison said again and again (for the issue in 1892 was high prices). ' There is such a thing, gentlemen, as having prices too low.' But the public did not heed the warning and we had four years of low prices.
Do you want to try this experiment again so soon ? We will have prices low enough as soon as the supply equals the demand, and the naked threat of a change of economic
policy always has had the effect to check demand more rapidly than anything else. Today consumers actually bid against each other.

It has often been pointed out that a protective policy will be a burden on the consumer ; and possibly to some extent during the building-up stages this may necessarily to some degree happen. But we have to pass through that stage, and the sooner we get past it and have the competition and the industries built up in our country, the better. Further on, using the United States Steel Corporation as an example, he says : The corporation Owns its own ore, and it therefore pays ou-t for labour directly or indirectly, every dollar exceipt what it pays in interest and dividends. It follows then that this one concern paid during the year ending June 30, 1902, directly or indirectly over $400,000,000 for labour. And what became of this money ? Most of it was spent primarily for food and raiment and material to build homes. This food came from the wheat fields of Minnesota and the Dakotas, and from the grazing fields of the south and from the sheep ranches of the far west, but it all came thence by way of the facifcorieis of New England and the Atlantic states. Nor is this all.

The farmers who received this money for food products, for cotton and for wool, spent it in turn for labour or for building material, for carpets, for clo-tlhling, or barbed wire, or nails, or other articles of consumption. The mills which ground the wheat, the packers who killed the beeves and the hogs, and the factory men who produced the cloth, paid at least 95 per cent of their gross receipts for labour.

And so these millions went on and on and on and are going still. They have cheered many homes. They have brought food to those who were starving six years ago, and they have helped, in a measure, to make us all rich. But what has the corporation done with its net profits ?
The stock of the corporation is held by more than 48,000 people. So this profit is thus divided and subdivided. And what do these stockholders do with it ? They, too, have been fed ail'd cloithed.

I speak of tfhese things only to show that the entire profit has not been lost. There are compensations, even with high prices. We have at least kept the money with us. It has not gone hence, and labour has received, perhaps niot its due proportion, but more than if the money had gone abroad.
But I believe competition is in sight. Bast year the entire rolled iron and steel product of the United States was 12,000 000 tons, of which the United

Corporation produced less than 51 per pent. The Lackawanna Iron and Steel Company is building a plant near Buffalo, costing $26,000,000, and they propose to he able to produce a mllUtoat and a quarter tons per annum. The independent concern, with which Mr. Frick in connected, is being increased to a $20,000,000 plant. I have a letter from Mr. James Swank, secretary of ""he American Iron and Steel Association, in which he says that when the plants now in process of construction are completed the of tllis countlT will be fully 24,000,000 tons per annum ; you can draw your own conclusions.

In my judgment w,e are to have competition, and it will be the kind the American people have learned to appreciate. It will be American competition, and our own1 artisans will not be forced upon the street again to beg while foreign workmen supply the limited needs of a paralyzed country.

I read this article with the object of showing you that the high protective system in the United States has proved a boon to that country. While there are necessarily some hardships in the working, it has fed and clothed their millions of workmen ; and while their prices are higher, they are able to pay their workmen higher wages. The people of the United States find that the protective system, when properly carried out, produces competition at home, which results in lower prices. That is what we want in this country. We want to establish a permanent and stable fiscal policy, which the people can have some dependence upon, instead of dribbling in bounties on one product or another, and having no definite line of action. The country would be in a very much better condition if we established some such policy and applied it to the steel industry, the lead industry and numerous other industries, which would come forward to reap the results which the hon. Minister of Customs expects them to reap from this measure, and they would have the added benefit of permanency.
